object_types.name: Incident
object_types.definition: A reported operational event requiring investigation and resolution, uniquely identified by an incident number and tracked through multiple states.

source_references.excerpt: Incident number. INC-, then a sequence.

object_types.name: IncidentNumber
object_types.definition: A unique identifier for an incident, formatted as INC- followed by a sequence number, never reused.

source_references.excerpt: Incident number. INC-, then a sequence... Unique. And we never delete incidents, which becomes relevant later.

object_types.name: Alert
object_types.definition: A notification generated by the monitoring platform when a system anomaly is detected, including manually-created alerts.

source_references.excerpt: Monitoring fires an alert... If an engineer spots something, they raise it, and raising it creates an alert record. It's a manual alert but it's still an alert.

object_types.name: AlertId
object_types.definition: A unique identifier for an alert, assigned by the monitoring platform.

source_references.excerpt: And an alert -- identified how? Alert ID. Comes from the monitoring platform.

object_types.name: Ticket
object_types.definition: A customer support request or issue report tracked in a different system from incidents.

source_references.excerpt: And a ticket has a ticket number. Different system, different format, always has.

object_types.name: TicketNumber
object_types.definition: A unique identifier for a ticket, from the support ticketing system.

source_references.excerpt: And a ticket has a ticket number. Different system, different format, always has.

object_types.name: Service
object_types.definition: A software system or operational component owned by a team, which may be affected by incidents.

source_references.excerpt: How is a service identified? Service name. They're unique, we enforce it in the catalogue.

object_types.name: ServiceName
object_types.definition: A unique name identifying a service, enforced to be unique in the service catalogue.

source_references.excerpt: How is a service identified? Service name. They're unique, we enforce it in the catalogue.

object_types.name: Team
object_types.definition: An organizational unit responsible for owning and maintaining services.

source_references.excerpt: Is a service owner a team or a person? A team. Services are owned by teams. People move.

object_types.name: TeamName
object_types.definition: A unique identifier for a team.

source_references.excerpt: Is a service owner a team or a person? A team. Services are owned by teams. People move.

object_types.name: Person
object_types.definition: An individual who may serve as an incident commander or be part of a team.

source_references.excerpt: The incident commander. One person, named, and it's a role for the duration, not a job title.

object_types.name: PersonId
object_types.definition: A unique identifier for a person.

source_references.excerpt: The incident commander. One person, named, and it's a role for the duration, not a job title.

object_types.name: Severity
object_types.definition: A classification of an incident's technical impact and blast radius, from SEV1 (complete outage) to SEV4 (cosmetic/degraded).

source_references.excerpt: SEV1 through SEV4. It's about blast radius and technical impact. SEV1 is everything's down for everyone. SEV4 is degraded, cosmetic, one region, nobody's really suffering.

object_types.name: Priority
object_types.definition: A classification of an incident's business urgency, customer impact, and SLA implications, from P1 (highest) to P4 (lowest), independent of severity.

source_references.excerpt: And priority is P1 through P4... Priority is about customer urgency. Who's affected, what they've promised their own customers, whether we're breaching an SLA.

object_types.name: IncidentState
object_types.definition: The current state of an incident, one of: Triage (initial assessment), Declared (confirmed and assigned commander), Mitigated (temporary fix applied), Resolved (permanent fix deployed), or Closed (incident complete).

ambiguities.description: Identification of Person: The transcript mentions that a person serves as an 'incident commander' but does not specify how individuals are uniquely identified in the system. Is there a person ID, employee number, email, or some other unique identifier? The reference_mode 'person_id' is inferred but not explicitly confirmed.

source_references.excerpt: The incident commander. One person, named, and it's a role for the duration, not a job title.

ambiguities.description: Team identification: While the transcript states that Services are owned by Teams and mentions Team names are unique within the context of service ownership, it is unclear whether Teams have a separate system-wide unique identifier (like a team_id) or whether the team name is the primary identifier. The reference_mode is inferred as 'team_name' but may need clarification.

source_references.excerpt: Is a service owner a team or a person? A team. Services are owned by teams. People move.

ambiguities.description: Severity changes over time: The transcript states that severity 'gets revised as we understand the blast radius' and that the history is kept 'in the timeline, as events' while 'the incident record carries the current severity.' This suggests the model should capture historical severity changes, but the current extraction only models the current severity value. Should severity history be tracked as a separate fact type or timeline entry?

source_references.excerpt: Severity gets revised as we understand the blast radius. That's normal and expected... In the timeline, as events. The incident record carries the current severity.

ambiguities.description: Priority vs Severity independence: While the transcript asserts that Priority and Severity are independent, it uses the examples of Halberd Financial (P1/SEV3) and a Sunday marketing site outage (SEV1/P4) to demonstrate cases. However, it is not entirely clear whether there are ANY business rules correlating these two dimensions (e.g., are there forbidden combinations?). The model assumes complete independence.

source_references.excerpt: Are they correlated at all? A P1 is always a SEV1... That is not true... And it goes the other way. We had a SEV1 at four in the morning on a Sunday where the affected surface was the marketing site. Everything down, nobody awake, no revenue impact. That was a P4.

ambiguities.description: Mandatory commander state transition: The transcript clarifies that triage incidents have no commander but declared incidents have exactly one. However, it does not explicitly state the rule for the other three states (mitigated, resolved, closed): when an incident transitions from declared to mitigated, does the commander assignment remain mandatory, or could it become optional in later states?

source_references.excerpt: Every incident has a commander? Yes... No, that's wrong, and I nearly gave you a rule we break constantly. An incident starts in triage. In triage there's no commander, that's the point of triage... Declared incidents have exactly one commander. Triage incidents have none.

ambiguities.description: Duplicate detection acyclicity: The transcript states that duplicate chains are 'wrong' and 'if C duplicates B and B duplicates A, then C should point at A' and that this is 'not enforced' today. Should the model include a ring-type constraint (acyclic) to formalize this rule, or is this a procedural/operational constraint outside the logical data model?

source_references.excerpt: Can a chain form? B duplicates A, C duplicates B? It shouldn't. The intent is that everything points at the primary directly. But nothing stops you making a chain and I've seen two-deep ones... It's wrong. If C duplicates B and B duplicates A, then C should point at A. When we roll up incident counts we only follow one hop, so a chain undercounts... That's the rule as intended. It's not enforced.

ambiguities.description: Customer-caused incident classification: The transcript extensively discusses a decision (deferred to Ravi) about whether incidents later found to be caused by customer misconfiguration should be reclassified, excluded from reliability metrics, or left unchanged. The model does not capture any cause classification because it 'isn't one to capture' today. Should the model include a placeholder for future cause classification, or is this correctly excluded as a future change?

source_references.excerpt: Support raises tickets. Some of those tickets become incidents. A meaningful number of those turn out to be user error... Whether an incident later found to be caused by customer misconfiguration should be reclassified, excluded from reliability metrics, or left as-is, is undecided. The model today captures the five states and does not include any concept of a cause classification, because there isn't one to capture.

ambiguities.description: Optionality of commander in declared state: While the transcript states 'Declared incidents have exactly one commander,' it does not clarify whether this mandatory assignment occurs at the instant of declaration or whether a brief interim period exists where an incident can be declared but not yet have a commander assigned. Is 'declared' a state that always includes a commander, or is commander assignment a separate action that must occur during or after declaration?

source_references.excerpt: Every incident has a commander? Yes... A commander is assigned when it's declared... Declared incidents have exactly one commander. Triage incidents have none.

ambiguities.description: Cardinality of affects relationship: The transcript states 'An incident affects one or more services. Usually one, sometimes several when it's an infrastructure thing.' This confirms an incident can affect multiple services. However, it does not clarify the reverse direction: can a service be affected by multiple incidents, or is each affected relationship one-to-one in that direction? The model assumes incidents can affect multiple services but does not constrain services to be affected by at most one incident.

source_references.excerpt: And an incident affects a service? One or more. Usually one, sometimes several when it's an infrastructure thing.

ambiguities.description: System identifiers for Alert and Ticket: The transcript mentions that Alert ID 'comes from the monitoring platform' and Ticket has 'a different system, different format.' It is unclear whether these identifiers are guaranteed to be globally unique across all systems or only unique within their respective systems. If they are only locally unique, composite keys combining system + id might be needed.

source_references.excerpt: And an alert -- identified how? Alert ID. Comes from the monitoring platform... And a ticket has a ticket number. Different system, different format, always has.

ambiguities.description: Deletion and historical tracking: The transcript states 'We never delete incidents, which becomes relevant later' but this relevance is never fully explained in the context of the data model. Does this imply that all incident history must be preserved, or is this only a business policy note? Should the model include any soft-delete or historical status tracking mechanism?

source_references.excerpt: Unique. And we never delete incidents, which becomes relevant later.
